description:
Wesam Saad explains irresistible grace as God’s effective work of giving new life. He rejects the picture of someone entering salvation while unwilling and forced: regeneration changes the person inwardly so that faith is a willing response. The terms monergism and synergism frame the discussion of divine action and human response. Romans 9 and John 1 support his argument that new birth originates in God rather than inherited status, human effort or an independent decision. Receiving Christ remains necessary in his explanation, while its enabling cause is distinguished from the response and the resulting right to belong to God’s family.

Questions about sowing the gospel lead to a discussion of the preacher’s external call and the Spirit’s internal work. Saad explains that hearing may precede a later response and that gospel communication can include written material rather than only an audible sermon. Passages about the necessity of new birth and the Father’s drawing are used to reject a separate route to saving faith without God’s call. The final section compares belief in 1 John 5 with love in 1 John 4, treating both as evidence of new birth, then discusses the verb tenses. The practical purpose is to understand and defend the teaching from Scripture while faithfully communicating the gospel.

questions.question: Does irresistible grace mean that a person is saved against their will?
questions.answer: Saad explicitly rejects that picture. He explains God’s effective calling as an inward change through regeneration, enabling the person willingly to repent and believe. The term concerns the effectiveness of God’s life-giving work rather than a struggle in which someone is dragged into heaven while refusing Christ.

questions.question: What question do monergism and synergism express in this session?
questions.answer: Saad uses the terms to ask whether new birth is God’s work or a cooperative production of God and an unregenerate person. He defends God as the source of regeneration while affirming the person’s actual response of receiving Christ. The argument does not remove responsibility to repent and believe.

questions.question: How does he use John 1:12–13?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes being born of God, receiving Christ, and receiving the right to become God’s children. He emphasises that birth is not attributed to ancestry, human effort or human will. In his interpretation, God’s life-giving action enables the response rather than being produced by an independent act of reception.

questions.question: How are the external and internal calls related?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes the gospel communicated by a person from the Spirit’s effective work. When someone comes to faith, he describes the proclamation and divine action working together in that event while remaining different agencies. He also allows a person to respond later while reflecting on the gospel already heard.

questions.question: Must the gospel be communicated through an audible sermon?
questions.answer: No. Saad explicitly includes written communication such as a tract. His emphasis is that the person receives the gospel’s content through communication, not that an audible ministerial voice is the only permissible medium. The explanation follows a question about people coming to faith in different circumstances.

questions.question: Why does he reject a separate route to faith without effective calling?
questions.answer: Saad appeals to the necessity of new birth in John 3 and the Father’s drawing and granting in John 6. He argues that the scope of these statements leaves no second class who come to saving faith entirely from themselves. His answer concerns the necessity of God’s action, not the irrelevance of believing.

questions.question: How does he compare belief in 1 John 5:1 with love in 1 John 4:7?
questions.answer: Saad treats the activities in those passages as identifying the person born of God rather than as independent achievements that produce new birth. He argues that the neighbouring love statement helps interpret the belief statement consistently. The discussion is about the passages’ spiritual description, not a claim that every ordinary human affection proves salvation.

questions.question: What part do the verb tenses play in his argument?
questions.answer: Saad contrasts the present believing with the perfect-tense description of being born of God, explaining the latter as a completed action with continuing effects. He uses this to support his reading of belief as the effect of new birth. This reports the teacher’s grammatical argument rather than asserting that a tense alone settles every theological question.

questions.question: How does he explain the language of planting a seed?
questions.answer: Saad relates it to the sower’s parable and to making the gospel known. The speaker does not know the final response or possess the power to create new life. The task is to communicate the word and pray for God to bring salvation, rather than treating the illustration as a guarantee of conversion.

questions.question: Which questions receive only limited treatment here?
questions.answer: The opening raises passages about human willingness, including Matthew 23:37 and Revelation 22:17. Saad affirms responsibility to receive Christ during the discussion, but does not give a full exposition of those passages here. The next topic is announced as perseverance of the saints; missing detailed answers are not supplied by this session.
